title: VLOOKUP vs INDEX MATCH: which lookup should you use?
intro: Every Excel user hits this fork: keep the one-liner VLOOKUP, or switch to the two-function INDEX + MATCH combo. VLOOKUP is shorter to write; INDEX + MATCH is structurally tougher — it survives column inserts, looks left, and returns positions as well as values.
verdict: Use VLOOKUP for quick, right-looking lookups in stable tables. Use INDEX + MATCH when the return column sits left of the key, when columns may be inserted, or when you need the match position — and if you have Microsoft 365, skip both and use XLOOKUP.

useLeftWhen: The key column is already leftmost and the table shape is fixed.

useRightWhen: The value you want sits left of the lookup column.
Columns get inserted or reordered in the source table.
You need the row position (for OFFSET, INDIRECT or further math).

title: VLOOKUP vs XLOOKUP: is it time to switch?
intro: XLOOKUP was designed to retire VLOOKUP. It defaults to exact match, searches any column in any direction, spills whole rows, and has a built-in 'if not found' argument — the only real blocker is that it requires Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+.
verdict: If every user of the workbook is on Microsoft 365 / Excel 2021+, use XLOOKUP — it is strictly better. Stay on VLOOKUP (or INDEX + MATCH) when the file must open in Excel 2016 or earlier.

rows.right: Safe — uses ranges, not an index

useLeftWhen: The workbook must run in Excel 2019 or older.
You're editing a legacy file and consistency matters more than features.
useRightWhen: Everyone on Microsoft 365 — exact-match default, left lookups, and no IFERROR wrapper.
You need to return a whole row or search bottom-up for the latest record.

title: SUMIF vs SUMIFS: one condition or many?
intro: SUMIF and SUMIFS differ by more than the trailing S — the argument order flips (the sum range is last in SUMIF, first in SUMIFS), and only SUMIFS accepts more than one criterion. Reach for the plural even with a single condition if you might add filters later.
verdict: Use SUMIF for a single condition and short formulas; use SUMIFS whenever you may need a second criterion — the extended form is identical in power and more future-proof.

rows.right: Every range must match exactly or #VALUE!

useLeftWhen: You have exactly one condition and want the shortest formula.
useRightWhen: You need two or more filters — region AND month AND amount.
The report will grow new criteria; upgrading SUMIF later is fiddly.

title: COUNT vs COUNTA: what does each one actually count?
intro: COUNT and COUNTA answer different questions: COUNT tallies numeric cells only, while COUNTA tallies anything non-empty. Picking the wrong one quietly over- or under-counts — the classic sign is a 'row count' that includes header text or a 'response count' that skips text answers.
verdict: Use COUNT for columns that should be purely numeric (amounts, scores, quantities). Use COUNTA for completeness checks — 'how many rows were filled in'.
useLeftWhen: The column is meant to hold numbers and text there is a data bug.
You're averaging or summing the same range — COUNT stays consistent.
useRightWhen: You want 'how many rows have anything' — form responses, name lists.
The column mixes types on purpose.

title: IF vs IFS: nested branches or a flat list?
intro: One test, two outcomes — IF is perfect. Three or more outcomes — nested IFs get hard to audit fast ('which parenthesis closes which branch?'), and IFS replaces them with a flat test/result list that stops at the first TRUE.
verdict: Use IF for a single binary decision. Use IFS for three-plus branches — but only on Excel 2019 / Microsoft 365; older files need nested IF.
useLeftWhen: The file must open in Excel 2016 or earlier.
useRightWhen: You have grade bands, status maps or tiered pricing.
Readability matters — auditors can scan IFS top to bottom.

title: CONCAT vs TEXTJOIN: joining text the right way
intro: Both join text — the difference is the delimiter. CONCAT glues items directly together; TEXTJOIN puts a separator between them and can skip empty cells, which is what 'a, b, c' lists and CSV exports actually need.
verdict: Use TEXTJOIN whenever items need a separator or the list may contain blanks; use CONCAT (or just &) when pieces bolt together with nothing between.

useLeftWhen: You want to mix literals and ranges freely.
useRightWhen: You're building comma-separated or dashed lists.
Some cells may be empty and you don't want stray delimiters.

title: LEFT vs MID: slicing text from the start or the middle
intro: LEFT takes a fixed-length prefix; MID takes a slice from any position. Many jobs that look like LEFT tasks — 'everything before the dash' — are really MID/FIND territory once the prefix length varies.
verdict: Use LEFT for fixed-width prefixes; use MID (with FIND to locate the start) when the piece you want sits at a variable position.
useLeftWhen: You need the first N characters and N is constant — country codes, prefixes.
useRightWhen: The target sits after a delimiter or at a computed position — domains, middle segments.

title: COUNTIF vs COUNTIFS: counting with one test or several
intro: COUNTIF counts cells matching one criterion; COUNTIFS stacks range/criteria pairs so every test must pass. Unlike SUMIF→SUMIFS the argument order stays the same — criteria always follow their range — so upgrading is painless.
verdict: Use COUNTIF for one condition; use COUNTIFS for anything more — or when the report might gain a second filter later.

title: FILTER vs lookup functions: one match or all of them?
intro: Lookups return the first match and stop; FILTER returns every matching row as a spill range. If your question is 'which rows', not 'which value', you want FILTER — the catch is it needs Microsoft 365.
verdict: Use FILTER when you need all matching rows and you're on Microsoft 365. Use VLOOKUP / INDEX+MATCH for single-cell answers and older Excel versions.
